newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica moves to halt wine co-op KWV privatisation.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica moves to halt wine co-op KWV privatisation.

text.p: South African Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom on Thursday moved to block plans by wine co-operative KWV to become a private company.
He said the bid would be delayed until he was satisfied that it was in the best interests of the wine industry.

The move, which follows intense behind-the-scenes negotiations, came as the co-operative was due to apply in the Cape Town Supreme Court for the Wine and Spirits Control Act to be amended to allow it to become a private company.
Hanekom said in a statement that he planned to apply for an order that would delay "the timetable anticipated by the KWV for their restructuring."
Hanekom said he had decided to obtain the order because he wanted to "ensure that a proper regulatory framework is in place with regard to the wine and distilling industry.
"The present application by the KWV threatens the integrity of the existing system," he said.

"I am concerned that monies and resources which were accumulated for the purposes of the KWV's regulatory function might be distributed amongst present KWV members as part of their scheme of arrangement."
He said he hoped that the matter could be resolved between the parties and all other stakeholders without the need for litigation.

It it could be settled by agreement or the courts make an appropriate ruling, Hanekom said he would begin as soon as possible consultations with the industry on meeting the needs of the KWV as well as those of the industry and public.

The KWV, which is believed to have assets of about two billion rand, last week announced that 4,751 of its members had approved a plan to convert the co-operative into a company from the end of April next year.
But several wine industry analysts have expressed concern about the plan as KWV has been a statutory body and has built up its assets on the basis of the control it had over the industry.
KWV chairman Lourens Jonker said last week that KWV would continue to be responsible for the administration and stabilisation of the wine industry and "remain the mouthpiece of the wine farmer".
Analysts have questioned whether, as a private company, it could in fact remain the industry regulator and speculation has been rife that Hanekom would be forced to act.

Analysts were particularly concerned that KWV's assets would be distributed to its members, most of whom have mainly been producers of distilling wine and have not contributed greatly to South Africa's drive to become a quality wine producer.
